title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how education should respond to the rapid introduction of AI tools such as ChatGPT, with particular emphasis on three skills the author argues are essential for modern education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is motivated by concerns that students and teachers may use AI uncritically, misunderstand its limitations, rely on hallucinated content, or offload too much cognitive work to AI. It also discusses institutional uncertainty about whether AI should be banned, unrestricted, or regulated through a middle-ground approach.

The paper does not study ChatGPT-generated feedback on student-authored drafts, nor does it report an intervention evaluating writing outcomes. Instead, it presents a conceptual discussion informed by informal, unstructured discussions at a Swiss university of applied sciences and a narrative review of relevant literature. A central illustrative case describes how the university developed internal AI guidelines permitting AI use in academic writing under conditions of transparency, critical evaluation, and prohibition of verbatim copying. The paper also outlines possible institutional supports such as workshops, AI literacy courses, and staff development, and it summarizes prompt engineering methods as pedagogical tools.

The population and context are primarily higher education, specifically students and staff at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland. Although the author suggests some ideas may also be useful for children, the actual case material and recommendations are centered on adult learners in university settings rather than K-12 students. No secondary-school sample, no grades 9-12 writing class, and no draft-feedback implementation are reported.

The main conclusion is that education should neither prohibit nor fully uncritically embrace AI, but instead cultivate a broader AI culture grounded in literacy about AI systems, deliberate instruction in prompt engineering, and strong critical thinking. The author argues that written AI guidelines alone are insufficient and should be complemented by training, workshops, curricular integration, and institutional resources. For the specific retrieval topic, evidence is absent: the paper reports no subgroup or moderator analyses by baseline writing proficiency, English learner status, disability, grade level, gender, achievement level, subject area, or genre; no follow-up or delayed posttest evidence on unaided writing after feedback removal; and no direct empirical findings on independent revision skill, self-efficacy, confidence, metacognition, authorial voice, plagiarism outcomes, or overreliance in secondary students receiving ChatGPT feedback on drafts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a conceptual discussion with a narrative literature review and informal, unstructured case-based observations from a higher-education setting. It does not provide a clear empirical design, K-12 sample, draft-feedback intervention study, or credible causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important implications for AI literacy, critical thinking, and institutional policy, but impact is unclear because no direct student outcome effects are measured and no effect sizes are reported.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of ChatGPT and similar large language models as classroom tools, academic work supports, and conversational sparring partners for students; includes guidance on prompt engineering, AI literacy, and institutional rules for student use in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues conceptually that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are necessary skills for effective educational use of ChatGPT-like systems, and it proposes workshops, courses, and institutional supports to develop them. However, it reports no formal empirical evaluation, no sample-based outcome data, and no effect sizes; claims are based on unstructured discussions at a Swiss university and a narrative literature review rather than measured student gains.
finding.measure: Informal attitudes and perceptions from unstructured discussions; no validated durable-skills outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes a Swiss university case study in which AI guidelines were created to allow restricted, transparent use of generative AI in student work, including documentation of model used, purpose, critical evaluation, and manuscript locations. The author identifies implementation challenges—student noncompliance, lack of training, limited monitoring capacity, and absence of dedicated staffing or budget—but provides no institutional outcome data or causal estimates.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline description and implementation challenges; no quantitative institutional outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively suggests that AI tools may improve efficiency for tasks such as curriculum creation, brainstorming, case-study construction, and academic writing support, while also noting time costs, training burdens, and uncertainty about proper use. These claims are illustrative and anecdotal, with no direct efficiency metrics, comparative analysis, or reported effect sizes.
finding.measure: Anecdotal descriptions of perceived efficiency/productivity in teaching and academic tasks; no formal efficiency metric reported
